claim: Platelet aggregates are involved in pathological thrombosis.
source: In addition to their participation in physiological hemostasis (Michelson, 2012; George, 2000; Michelson, 2003; Harrison, 2005), platelet aggregates are also involved in pathological thrombosis (Davì and Patrono, 2007; Ruggeri, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on platelet involvement in thrombosis.

claim: Inflammation, atherosclerosis, and cancer metastasis are closely associated with platelet aggregation.
source: Moreover, it is known that a range of diseases or medical conditions, such as inflammation, atherosclerosis, and cancer metastasis, are closely associated with platelet aggregation (Lievens and von Hundelshausen, 2011; Engelmann and Massberg, 2013; Franco et al., 2015; Gay and Felding-Habermann, 2011).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to literature on disease associations with platelet aggregation.

claim: Long-term foreign body contact of blood with artificial devices in extracorporeal circulation often leads to platelet aggregation and thrombus formation followed by serious complications.
source: Also, in patients with artificial lungs due to severe respiratory failure such as the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) caused by severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) (Ramanathan et al., 2020; Ronco et al., 2020), the long-term foreign body contact of blood with the artificial devices in the extracorporeal circulation often leads to platelet aggregation and thrombus formation followed by serious complications (e.g., myocardial infarction, cerebral infarction) (Brodie et al., 2019; Brodie and Bacchetta, 2011; Oliver, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on complications from artificial lung devices.

claim: Platelet aggregation is elicited by a variety of agonists which bind to and activate specific receptors expressed on the platelet.
source: Here, the aggregation of platelets is elicited by a variety of agonists, which bind to and activate specific receptors expressed on the platelet.
evidence: Draws from established knowledge of platelet activation mechanisms.

claim: Agonist binding leads to platelet activation and structural and functional changes of glycoprotein IIb/IIIa expressed on the platelet surface.
source: This leads to platelet activation and structural and functional changes of glycoprotein IIb/IIIa expressed on the platelet surface.
evidence: Draws from established knowledge of platelet activation pathways.

claim: The activated form of glycoprotein IIb/IIIa can bind with fibrinogen, enabling platelets to interact with each other and form aggregates.
source: The activated form of the glycoprotein can bind with fibrinogen, enabling platelets to interact with each other and form aggregates (Michelson, 2012; George, 2000; Michelson, 2003; Harrison, 2005; Moser et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on platelet aggregation mechanisms.

claim: Platelet aggregates look morphologically similar and have long been thought indistinguishable since the discovery of platelet aggregates in the 19th century.
source: Despite the existence of diverse agonist types, platelet aggregates look morphologically similar and have long been thought indistinguishable since the discovery of platelet aggregates in the 19th century (Michelson, 2012; George, 2000; Michelson, 2003; Harrison, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature and historical context of platelet research.

claim: Morphological characteristics of platelet aggregates on a large statistical scale have been overlooked because microscopy has been the only method to examine them.
source: This is because morphological characteristics of platelet aggregates on a large statistical scale have been overlooked as microscopy (a high-content, but low-throughput tool) has been the only method to examine them (Finsterbusch et al., 2018; Nitta et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations and logical inference about limitations of microscopy.

claim: The study presents an intelligent method for classifying platelet aggregates by agonist type.
source: In this Short Report, we present an intelligent method for classifying platelet aggregates by agonist type.
evidence: This is the primary claim of the study, supported by the experimental data presented throughout.

claim: The classification method is enabled by performing high-throughput imaging flow cytometry of numerous blood cells, training a convolutional neural network with the image data, and using the CNN to identify and differentiate subtle yet appreciable morphological features of platelet aggregates activated by different types of agonists.
source: This is enabled by performing high-throughput imaging flow cytometry of numerous blood cells, training a convolutional neural network (CNN) with the image data, and using the CNN to identify and differentiate subtle yet appreciable morphological features of platelet aggregates activated by different types of agonists.
evidence: Describes the methodology used in the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: Platelet aggregates can be classified by agonist type through their morphology, which is unprecedented and has never been reported previously.
source: Our finding that platelet aggregates can be classified by agonist type through their morphology is unprecedented as it has never been reported previously.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the experimental results.

claim: Information about the driving factors behind the formation of platelet aggregates is expected to lead to a better understanding of the underlying mechanism of platelet aggregation.
source: The information about the driving factors behind the formation of platelet aggregates is expected to lead to a better understanding of the underlying mechanism of platelet aggregation and open a window on an entirely new class of clinical diagnostics, pharmacometrics, and therapeutics.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the potential impact of the findings.

claim: ADP, collagen, TRAP-6, and U46619 are commonly used in platelet aggregation tests.
source: Here, adenosine diphosphate (ADP), collagen, thrombin receptor activator peptide-6 (TRAP-6), and U46619 were used since they are commonly used in platelet aggregation tests (Michelson, 2012; George, 2000; Michelson, 2003; Harrison, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on platelet aggregation testing.

claim: The concentrations of the agonists were carefully chosen to minimize variations in aggregate size between the different blood sample portions.
source: Initially, the concentrations of the agonists were carefully chosen (20 µM for ADP, 10 µg/mL for collagen, 13 µM for TRAP-6, 14 µM for U46619) to minimize variations in aggregate size between the different blood sample portions.
evidence: Describes the experimental design rationale.

claim: Images were acquired through six experimental trials to mitigate potential bias in the dataset that may have come from experimental variations.
source: These images were acquired through six experimental trials (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) to mitigate potential bias in the dataset that may have come from experimental variations (e.g., signal-to-noise ratio, fluctuations in optical alignment, hydrodynamic cell focusing conditions, sample preparation).
evidence: Describes the experimental design to reduce bias, supported by reference to figure.

claim: Four different concentrations of each agonist were used for platelet activation to examine the potential influence of agonist concentrations on the ability to differentiate platelet aggregates by agonist type.
source: Then, four different concentrations of each agonist (2, 5, 10, 20 µM for ADP, 1, 5, 10, 20 µg/mL for collagen, 1, 5, 13, 20 µM for TRAP-6, 2.8, 5.6, 14, 28 µM for U46619) were used for platelet activation to examine the potential influence of agonist concentrations on the ability to differentiate platelet aggregates by agonist type, where the concentrations were chosen by referring to the concentrations of agonists used in light transmission aggregometry and in vitro flow-cytometric platelet aggregation tests (Koltai et al., 2017; Granja et al., 2015).
evidence: Describes the experimental design with citation support for concentration choices.

claim: The platelet aggregates were enriched by density-gradient centrifugation to remove erythrocytes from the blood sample portions.
source: The platelet aggregates were enriched by density-gradient centrifugation to remove erythrocytes from the blood sample portions.
evidence: Describes the sample preparation method used in the study.

claim: 2% paraformaldehyde was added to the blood sample portions to fix them and prevent the platelet aggregates from dissolving during imaging flow cytometry.
source: To prevent the platelet aggregates from dissolving during imaging flow cytometry, 2% paraformaldehyde was added to the blood sample portions to fix them.
evidence: Describes the sample preparation method and its rationale.

claim: The current sample preparation procedure is advantageous over other procedures in preserving the morphology of platelet aggregates.
source: In addition to this sample preparation procedure, we tested other procedures such as pipetting, vortexing, fixation, and non-fixation and identified the current procedure to be advantageous over the others in preserving the morphology of platelet aggregates (Figure 1—figure supplement 3; Materials and methods).
evidence: Supported by comparison with other methods and reference to figure showing results.

claim: An optofluidic time-stretch microscope was employed for high-throughput, blur-free, bright-field image acquisition of events in each sample portion.
source: Second, an optofluidic time-stretch microscope (Goda et al., 2009; Jiang et al., 2017; Lei et al., 2018; Lau et al., 2016) was employed for high-throughput, blur-free, bright-field image acquisition of events (e.g., single platelets, platelet-platelet aggregates, platelet-leukocyte aggregates, single leukocytes, cell debris, remaining erythrocytes) in each sample portion (Figure 1—figure supplements 4 and 5; Materials and methods).
evidence: Describes the imaging method with citations and reference to figures.

claim: Fluorescence image acquisition is not needed because fluorescence images of platelet aggregates would look very similar to their bright-field images except for the colors.
source: Here, fluorescence image acquisition is not needed because fluorescence images of platelet aggregates would look very similar to their bright-field images (except for the colors).
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity of information content between imaging modalities.

claim: Two CNN models were trained to classify platelets based on their morphological features by agonist type.
source: Third, the acquired images of the events were used to train two CNN models that classified the platelets based on their morphological features by agonist type (Figure 1B).
evidence: Describes the machine learning approach used in the study.

claim: The first CNN model was trained with images of platelet aggregates activated by certain concentrations of agonists (12,000 images per agonist type) to examine their morphological changes while minimizing a potential influence of concentration-dependent factors.
source: Specifically, we first trained a CNN model with images of platelet aggregates activated by certain concentrations of agonists (12,000 images per agonist type) in order to examine their morphological changes while minimizing a potential influence of concentration-dependent factors on the morphology of the platelet aggregates.
evidence: Describes the training approach for the first CNN model.

claim: The second CNN model was trained with a dataset in which the images of platelet aggregates activated by different concentrations of the agonists were equally mixed (12,000 images in total per agonist type) to show that different concentrations of the agonists do not perturb the CNN model's ability to classify platelet aggregates.
source: Then, we trained the other CNN model with a dataset in which the images of platelet aggregates activated by different concentrations of the agonists were equally mixed (12,000 images in total per agonist type) in order to show that different concentrations of the agonists do not perturb the CNN model's ability to classify platelet aggregates.
evidence: Describes the training approach for the second CNN model and its purpose.

claim: The CNN with an encoder-decoder architecture was employed to disregard insignificant features such as background noise and keep important features in the bottleneck layer.
source: We employed the CNN (Krizhevsky et al., 2012) with an encoder-decoder architecture to disregard insignificant features such as background noise and keep important features in the bottleneck layer and trained it with the data of a single blood donor to ensure that only the morphological features driven by the agonists contributed to the development of the iPAC (Figure 1C; Materials and methods).
evidence: Describes the CNN architecture choice with citation and rationale.

claim: The CNN was trained with data of a single blood donor to ensure that only the morphological features driven by the agonists contributed to the development of the iPAC.
source: We employed the CNN (Krizhevsky et al., 2012) with an encoder-decoder architecture to disregard insignificant features such as background noise and keep important features in the bottleneck layer and trained it with the data of a single blood donor to ensure that only the morphological features driven by the agonists contributed to the development of the iPAC (Figure 1C; Materials and methods).
evidence: Describes the experimental design rationale to isolate agonist-driven features.

claim: A conventional flow cytometer was not capable of differentiating platelet samples prepared under the same procedure as indicated by their significant overlap.
source: In comparison, we measured the platelet samples that were prepared under the same procedure using a conventional flow cytometer (Cytomics FC500, Beckman Coulter) which is based on fluorescence measurements for cell classification. As shown in Figure 2, the flow cytometer was not capable of differentiating them as indicated by their significant overlap (Figure 2—source data 1; Materials and methods).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Most of the images were classified into the correct groups in the diagonal line of the confusion matrix.
source: As shown in Figure 3A, most of the images were classified into the correct groups in the diagonal line of the confusion matrix.
evidence: Supported by the confusion matrix data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Large separations between the different platelet sample portions in the t-SNE plot indicate the first CNN model's ability to discriminate various types of agonist-activated platelet aggregates and negative control.
source: Large separations between the different platelet sample portions in Figure 3B that visualizes the bottleneck layer in the CNN indicate the first CNN model's ability to discriminate various types of agonist-activated platelet aggregates and negative control (Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by the t-SNE visualization shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The negative control shows the highest classification accuracy, indicating that large morphological changes were made to the activated platelets.
source: The negative control shows the highest classification accuracy, indicating that large morphological changes were made to the activated platelets.
evidence: Inference drawn from the classification accuracy data.

claim: The U46619-treated blood sample portion shows the second highest classification accuracy of all the blood sample portions, indicating that the morphological changes caused by the agonist are very different from those caused by the other agonists.
source: The U46619-treated blood sample portion shows the second highest classification accuracy of all the blood sample portions, indicating that the morphological changes caused by the agonist are very different from those caused by the other agonists.
evidence: Inference drawn from the classification accuracy data.

claim: Many platelet-leukocyte aggregates were identified in the U46619-treated sample portion, but few in the other blood sample portions.
source: Many platelet-leukocyte aggregates were identified in the U46619-treated sample portion, but few in the other blood sample portions (Figure 2).
evidence: Supported by observations from Figure 2.

claim: U46619 acted as a thromboxane A2 (TXA2) receptor agonist, which activated TXA2 receptors that are abundantly expressed on platelets, vascular smooth muscle cells, and injured vascular endothelial cells.
source: This may be because U46619 acted as a thromboxane A2 (TXA2) receptor agonist, which activated TXA2 receptors that are abundantly expressed on platelets, vascular smooth muscle cells, and injured vascular endothelial cells.
evidence: Draws from established knowledge of U46619 mechanism of action.

claim: The activation of TXA2 receptors may affect the morphology of U46619-induced platelet aggregates by promoting the expression of adhesion molecules that favors the adhesion and infiltration of leukocytes.
source: The activation of TXA2 receptors may affect the morphology of U46619-induced platelet aggregates by promoting the expression of adhesion molecules that favors the adhesion and infiltration of leukocytes (Michelson, 2012; George, 2000).
evidence: Speculative explanation supported by citations to literature.

claim: The low classification accuracy values of the ADP-, collagen-, and TRAP-6-treated blood sample portions are presumably due to the fact that these agonists partially share similar mechanisms in forming platelets aggregates.
source: The low classification accuracy values of the ADP-, collagen-, and TRAP-6-treated blood sample portions are presumably due to the fact that these agonists partially share similar mechanisms in forming platelets aggregates (Michelson, 2012; George, 2000; Michelson, 2003; Harrison, 2005; Li et al., 2000).
evidence: Inference based on classification results and cited literature on platelet mechanisms.

claim: Platelets release ADP themselves during activation.
source: For example, since platelets also release ADP themselves during activation (Michelson, 2012; George, 2000; Michelson, 2003; Harrison, 2005), platelet aggregates produced by other agonists may also share similar morphological features as ADP-activated platelet aggregates.
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on platelet activation.

claim: Platelet aggregates produced by other agonists may share similar morphological features as ADP-activated platelet aggregates.
source: For example, since platelets also release ADP themselves during activation (Michelson, 2012; George, 2000; Michelson, 2003; Harrison, 2005), platelet aggregates produced by other agonists may also share similar morphological features as ADP-activated platelet aggregates.
evidence: Inference based on the fact that platelets release ADP during activation.

claim: TRAP-6 activates thrombin receptors while thrombin generation may be amplified by other agonists during platelet activation.
source: In addition, TRAP-6 activates thrombin receptors while thrombin generation may be amplified by other agonists during platelet activation (Mann, 2011), which indicates that the low prediction values of TRAP-6 can be attributed to the participation of thrombin in platelet aggregation induced by all types of agonists.
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on thrombin generation.

claim: The low prediction values of TRAP-6 can be attributed to the participation of thrombin in platelet aggregation induced by all types of agonists.
source: In addition, TRAP-6 activates thrombin receptors while thrombin generation may be amplified by other agonists during platelet activation (Mann, 2011), which indicates that the low prediction values of TRAP-6 can be attributed to the participation of thrombin in platelet aggregation induced by all types of agonists.
evidence: Inference based on the mechanism of TRAP-6 and thrombin involvement.

claim: Platelets are commonly simultaneously activated by multiple agonists whose effects on platelet aggregation are coupled.
source: Furthermore, it is common that platelets are simultaneously activated by multiple agonists whose effects on platelet aggregation are coupled whereas they are also influenced by other factors such as locally produced inhibitors, vascular endothelial cells, blood flow, and coagulation proteins during activation (Cattaneo and Lecchi, 2007; Michelson, 2012), thereby leading to the low classification accuracy values of certain agonists, which can be overcome by including the influences into the classification model to cover a wide spectrum of aggregation factors.
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on platelet activation complexity.

claim: Platelets are influenced by other factors such as locally produced inhibitors, vascular endothelial cells, blood flow, and coagulation proteins during activation.
source: Furthermore, it is common that platelets are simultaneously activated by multiple agonists whose effects on platelet aggregation are coupled whereas they are also influenced by other factors such as locally produced inhibitors, vascular endothelial cells, blood flow, and coagulation proteins during activation (Cattaneo and Lecchi, 2007; Michelson, 2012), thereby leading to the low classification accuracy values of certain agonists, which can be overcome by including the influences into the classification model to cover a wide spectrum of aggregation factors.
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on factors affecting platelet activation.

claim: The low classification accuracy values of certain agonists can be overcome by including the influences into the classification model to cover a wide spectrum of aggregation factors.
source: Furthermore, it is common that platelets are simultaneously activated by multiple agonists whose effects on platelet aggregation are coupled whereas they are also influenced by other factors such as locally produced inhibitors, vascular endothelial cells, blood flow, and coagulation proteins during activation (Cattaneo and Lecchi, 2007; Michelson, 2012), thereby leading to the low classification accuracy values of certain agonists, which can be overcome by including the influences into the classification model to cover a wide spectrum of aggregation factors.
evidence: Speculative statement about potential improvements to the model.

claim: The contribution values over all the agonists are in good agreement with the values in the diagonal elements of the confusion matrix, which validates the reliability of the iPAC.
source: The contribution values over all the agonists are in good agreement with the values in the diagonal elements of the confusion matrix (Figure 3C), which validates the reliability of the iPAC.
evidence: Supported by comparison of validation data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The iPAC's ability to classify platelet aggregates by agonist type in a concentration-independent manner is indicated by the confusion matrix with an average diagonal element value of 77%.
source: The iPAC's ability to classify platelet aggregates by agonist type in a concentration-independent manner is indicated by the confusion matrix shown in Figure 3D with an average diagonal element value of 77%.
evidence: Supported by the confusion matrix data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The results reveal the existence of unique morphological features related to each agonist type.
source: The results also reveal the existence of the unique morphological features related to each agonist type, which is promising for potential application to diagnosis of thrombotic disorders by tracing back to the leading factors of platelet aggregation.
evidence: Inference drawn from the classification results.

claim: The iPAC can quantify platelet aggregability with the resolving power to identify the contribution of each agonist type to it, while conventional assays can only evaluate platelet aggregability qualitatively.
source: In addition, from a viewpoint of potential clinical applications, while the conventional assays can only evaluate platelet aggregability qualitatively, the iPAC can quantify it with the resolving power to identify the contribution of each agonist type to it.
evidence: Comparison between iPAC and conventional methods based on their capabilities.

claim: U46619-activated platelet aggregates have relatively larger size than those in the other sample portions, which may be captured as a type of morphological features by the CNN, leading to the high classification accuracy of the U46619-activated samples.
source: However, it can be recognized from the image library (Figure 1B) that U46619-activated platelet aggregates have relatively larger size than those in the other sample portions, which may be captured as a type of morphological features by the CNN, leading to the high classification accuracy of the U46619-activated samples.
evidence: Observation from images and inference about CNN feature detection.

claim: Over 85% of the total population of platelets in all the samples were identified as single platelets, which indicates the ability of the iPAC to differentiate single platelets and platelet aggregates.
source: Over 85% of the total population of platelets in all the samples were identified as single platelets, which indicates the ability of the iPAC to differentiate single platelets and platelet aggregates.
evidence: Supported by the classification results from blood samples of healthy subjects.

claim: The agonist types of the platelet aggregates in each subject's platelet classification results are consistent between the repeated experiments, indicating that the variations between the subjects resulted from platelet heterogeneity, not test variations.
source: Furthermore, the agonist types of the platelet aggregates in each subject's platelet classification results are consistent between the repeated experiments, indicating that the variations between the subjects resulted from platelet heterogeneity, not test variations.
evidence: Inference drawn from the consistency of repeated experimental results.

claim: The iPAC holds promise for clinical diagnostics, pharmacometrics, and therapeutics, although it needs more training with a wide spectrum of diseases and medical conditions for the purpose.
source: The iPAC's diagnostic ability to obtain this type of information is an effective tool for studying and elucidating the mechanism of platelet aggregation and holds promise for clinical diagnostics, pharmacometrics, and therapeutics, although the iPAC needs more training with a wide spectrum of diseases and medical conditions for the purpose.
evidence: Speculative statement about future potential with acknowledgment of current limitations.

claim: The iPAC may provide an important clue to the choice of drugs for antiplatelet therapy.
source: For example, the iPAC may provide an important clue to the choice of drugs (e.g., aspirin or thienopyridines) for antiplatelet therapy (Mauri et al., 2014; Roe et al., 2012), the gold standard of the treatment and prevention of atherothrombosis (e.g., myocardial infarction, cerebral infarction), in that aspirin inhibits the formation of TXA2 whose stable analogue is U46619 while thienopyridines exert an antiplatelet effect by blocking the ADP receptor P2Y12.
evidence: Speculative application supported by citations to literature on antiplatelet therapy.

claim: Aspirin inhibits the formation of TXA2 whose stable analogue is U46619.
source: For example, the iPAC may provide an important clue to the choice of drugs (e.g., aspirin or thienopyridines) for antiplatelet therapy (Mauri et al., 2014; Roe et al., 2012), the gold standard of the treatment and prevention of atherothrombosis (e.g., myocardial infarction, cerebral infarction), in that aspirin inhibits the formation of TXA2 whose stable analogue is U46619 while thienopyridines exert an antiplatelet effect by blocking the ADP receptor P2Y12.
evidence: Draws from established knowledge of aspirin mechanism of action.

claim: Thienopyridines exert an antiplatelet effect by blocking the ADP receptor P2Y12.
source: For example, the iPAC may provide an important clue to the choice of drugs (e.g., aspirin or thienopyridines) for antiplatelet therapy (Mauri et al., 2014; Roe et al., 2012), the gold standard of the treatment and prevention of atherothrombosis (e.g., myocardial infarction, cerebral infarction), in that aspirin inhibits the formation of TXA2 whose stable analogue is U46619 while thienopyridines exert an antiplatelet effect by blocking the ADP receptor P2Y12.
evidence: Draws from established knowledge of thienopyridine mechanism of action.

claim: Antiplatelet therapy is the gold standard of the treatment and prevention of atherothrombosis.
source: For example, antiplatelet therapy is the gold standard of the treatment and prevention of atherothrombosis (e.g., myocardial infarction, cerebral infarction) for which aspirin and thienopyridines (e.g., prasugrel and clopidogrel) are primarily used as antiplatelet drugs worldwide (Mauri et al., 2014; Roe et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on antiplatelet therapy.

claim: The iPAC may be able to identify TRAP-6-activated platelet aggregates in the bloodstream of patients with deep vein thrombosis and suggest that they come from the venous side.
source: Furthermore, the iPAC may be able to identify TRAP-6-activated platelet aggregates in the bloodstream of patients with deep vein thrombosis (since TRAP-6 interacts with the receptor of thrombin) and suggest that they come from the venous side.
evidence: Speculative application based on the mechanism of TRAP-6.

claim: Deep vein thrombosis is a blood clot that normally occurs in a deep vein where coagulation activation plays an important role.
source: Furthermore, deep vein thrombosis (DVT) is a blood clot that normally occurs in a deep vein where coagulation activation plays an important role.
evidence: Draws from established medical knowledge of DVT.

claim: TRAP-6 interacts with the receptor of thrombin.
source: Since TRAP-6 interacts with the receptor of thrombin (i.e., the product of the coagulation cascade), the ability to identify TRAP-6-activated platelet aggregates in the blood stream may suggest that aggregates come from the venous side.
evidence: Draws from established knowledge of TRAP-6 mechanism.

claim: The iPAC may pave the way for introducing a novel laboratory testing technique for the management of pathological thrombosis such as atherothrombosis and DVT although further basic and clinical studies are needed.
source: Therefore, the iPAC may pave the way for introducing a novel laboratory testing technique for the management of pathological thrombosis such as atherothrombosis and DVT although further basic and clinical studies are needed.
evidence: Speculative statement about future potential with acknowledgment of need for further studies.

claim: The relation between platelet activation signaling pathways and the formation of platelet aggregates has been extensively studied.
source: The relation between platelet activation signaling pathways and the formation of platelet aggregates has been extensively studied (Li et al., 2010; Michelson, 2012; Brass et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on platelet signaling.

claim: Agonists activate platelets in a selective manner via specific receptors, which is followed by a variety of downstream signaling events.
source: It is known that agonists activate platelets in a selective manner via specific receptors, which is followed by a variety of downstream signaling events (Li et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on platelet activation.

claim: Collagen interacts with the immune-like receptor glycoprotein VI, which signals through an immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activation motif and activates the tyrosine phosphorylation pathway.
source: For example, collagen interacts with the immune-like receptor glycoprotein VI, which signals through an immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activation motif and activates the tyrosine phosphorylation pathway (Michelson, 2012; Li et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on collagen-platelet interactions.

claim: Soluble agonists such as TRAP-6, U46619, and ADP interact with G protein-coupled receptors.
source: In contrast, soluble agonists such as TRAP-6, U46619, and ADP interact with G protein-coupled receptors (Michelson, 2012; Brass, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on platelet receptor interactions.

claim: Each soluble agonist couples with a specific type of G protein, which leads to different aggregation mechanisms.
source: Furthermore, each soluble agonist couples with a specific type of G protein, which leads to different aggregation mechanisms (Rivera et al., 2009) and thus suggests different underlying mechanisms for expressing different morphological features on platelet aggregates.
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on G protein coupling.

claim: Different G protein coupling suggests different underlying mechanisms for expressing different morphological features on platelet aggregates.
source: Furthermore, each soluble agonist couples with a specific type of G protein, which leads to different aggregation mechanisms (Rivera et al., 2009) and thus suggests different underlying mechanisms for expressing different morphological features on platelet aggregates.
evidence: Inference based on the relationship between G protein coupling and aggregation mechanisms.

claim: Blood samples were obtained from a healthy person with 3.2% citric acid as the anticoagulant.
source: Specifically, blood samples were obtained from a healthy person with 3.2% citric acid as the anticoagulant (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Describes the sample collection method used in the study.

claim: 3.2% citrate blood is desirable for clinical coagulation tests.
source: Although it has a depressed concentration of ionized calcium, 3.2% citrate blood is desirable for clinical coagulation tests (Adcock et al., 1997; Cazenave et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on blood collection for coagulation testing.

claim: Heparin and EDTA are not suitable for this study because they influence the coagulation functions of platelets.
source: The other common anticoagulants, such as heparin and ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA), are not suitable for this study because they influence the coagulation functions of platelets (Ludlam, 1981).
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on anticoagulant effects on platelets.

claim: Platelets were immunofluorescently labeled by adding 20 µL PE anti-human CD61 to the blood samples to ensure that platelets would be detected in all images.
source: Platelets were immunofluorescently labeled by adding 20 µL PE anti-human CD61 (BioLegend, 336405) to the blood samples to ensure that platelets would be detected in all images (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Describes the labeling method used in the study.

claim: The study was approved by the Institutional Ethics Committee in the School of Medicine at the University of Tokyo.
source: This study was approved by the Institutional Ethics Committee in the School of Medicine at the University of Tokyo [no. 11049-(6)].
evidence: Statement of ethical approval for the study.

claim: Written informed consents were obtained from the blood donors.
source: Written informed consents were obtained from the blood donors.
evidence: Statement of ethical compliance for the study.
